vignette:
He is 22, Latin American, and comes across as older than his age in some ways, as if the months after the war have pressed him into a different shape. He is single and works as a product manager now, a job that requires him to think in timelines, priorities, and trade-offs, but he speaks about his life as if there is a clean line between before and after, and everything since the violence began has been measured against that break.

He describes being caught in a war zone as a civilian while still trying to keep ordinary routines intact. Before the shelling became constant, he tells himself that he believed the sounds in the distance would stay distant. He was trying to get to work, checking messages, making plans, thinking like someone who expected tomorrow to arrive in a familiar way. Then the city changed. Streets that had once felt crowded and alive became places to move through quickly and with your head down. He remembers the first time he had to lie on the floor with strangers while explosions shook the building overhead, all of them listening for the next impact, trying to guess whether the walls would hold. He recalls the smell of dust and smoke, the strange intimacy of sharing silence with people he did not know, each person waiting to see whether the noise outside would become the noise inside.

Over time, fear becomes practical. He learns which route has less traffic, which hour is safest, which sounds mean to stay put and which mean to run. He begins making decisions almost automatically, scanning windows, counting exits, checking the sky. He says that even then he still tries to work when he can, answering messages on his phone and staying connected to his team because the routines feel like proof that he remains himself. Yet concentration becomes harder. He rereads the same sentence several times and finds that his mind has drifted to the nearest checkpoint, the last loud bang, the people he left behind that morning. His role as a product manager once felt like a way to build and organize things; in the war zone, it becomes a source of tension because planning for the future feels both necessary and unreal.

He eventually leaves, but leaving does not end the fear. In the safer place where he lives now, he is often surprised by how quickly his body reacts to sound. A door slamming in his apartment makes him freeze before he realizes where he is. Sirens, construction noise, even the sudden pop of a car backfiring can send a jolt through him that feels immediate and physical. He notices himself sitting with his back to a wall in restaurants, checking exits almost before he knows he has done it. He sleeps lightly and wakes quickly, sometimes with his heart racing, certain for a second that he has heard something dangerous. On nights when he does sleep through, he dreams of being trapped in the city again, moving through streets that never quite lead anywhere safe. He wakes tense, disoriented, and stays awake staring at the ceiling while his mind runs through fragments of memory he does not want.

He tries to explain that he is not only afraid of what happened, but of how unexpectedly present it still feels. Certain smells, certain images on the news, even a particular tone in someone's voice can pull him back to those days. When this happens, he becomes quiet and distant, as if part of him has stepped away. At other times, he feels irritable and on edge, especially when he is tired. He can seem detached with friends, not because he does not care, but because it takes effort to stay fully in the room. He misses the version of himself who moved through the world without calculating danger, and he grieves the ease he once took for granted. He still works hard and remains capable, but the cost is visible in the vigilance he carries everywhere, in the way his shoulders stay tight, in the way ordinary life now asks him to do something that once came naturally: believe he is safe enough to relax.
